subject: Science

unit.unitOverview: Look down at the ground beneath your feet. Right now you are standing on the outside of an enormous ball of rock and metal that is spinning through space. We call it the Earth. It is our home, and it is the only planet we know of where people, animals, plants, camels, birds and fish can all live together. In this unit you will become an Earth explorer. You will discover what the Earth is like deep inside, why some mountains spit out fire and hot rock, why the ground sometimes shakes, and how so many different living things find a home in different corners of our world.

outcomes: By the end of this unit, you will be able to:
Describe the three main layers of the Earth — the crust, the mantle and the core — and say what each layer is made of.
Explain how scientists use models to understand the inside of the Earth, and why a model is never a perfect copy of the real thing.
Describe how a volcano forms and name its main parts: the vent, the crater, the lava and the ash.
Explain what causes an earthquake and how the shaking travels as waves to the surface.
Describe how earthquakes under the sea can cause a tsunami (a giant sea wave).
Explain how animals and plants are suited to their habitat, using local examples such as the savanna, the coral reef and the mangrove.
Connect the Earth's hot inside layers to the volcanoes and earthquakes we see at the surface.
Here are the important words for this unit. Read them now, and come back to this table whenever you meet a word you have forgotten.
The thin, solid outer layer of the Earth where we live, made of rock.

concepts.title: The Structure of the Earth
concepts.explanation:
You already know quite a lot about the outside of the Earth. It is made of rocks, soil, sand, mountains, and the salty water of the seas and oceans. Scientists call this the Earth's external structure — 'external' just means 'outside'. When you walk across the savanna near Garissa, or feel the sand of the Indian Ocean coast at Kismaayo, you are touching the external structure of the Earth.

But what about the parts we cannot see — the parts deep inside the Earth? These make up the Earth's internal structure ('internal' means 'inside'). Here is a big problem for scientists: nobody can cut the Earth in half to look inside! The deepest hole that humans have ever drilled goes down only about 12 km, and yet the Earth is thousands of kilometres deep. So how can we possibly know what is down there?

The answer is that scientists use a model. A model is a way of showing or explaining something that we cannot easily see. You use models all the time without knowing it. A toy camel is a model of a real camel. A drawing of your house is a model of your house. Models help us understand and picture things — but a model is never a perfect, true copy of the real thing. A toy camel cannot walk, chew or give milk!

To imagine the inside of the Earth, think about a peach (or a mango, which may be easier to find near you). A whole mango has smooth skin on the outside. But if you cut it open, you see it has different layers inside: the soft juicy fruit, and then the hard stone in the very middle. The Earth is a little bit like this. It has a thin skin on the outside and different layers hidden inside, all the way down to a hard centre. Cutting the mango is a model that helps us picture what we would see if we could slice the Earth in half.

Did You Know? The temperature inside the Earth gets hotter and hotter the deeper you go. This is why deep gold mines in Africa are extremely hot to work in — the miners are getting closer to the Earth's burning-hot inside!

Scientists tell us the Earth has three main layers. Let us travel from the top all the way down to the centre.

1. The Crust. This is the thin, solid outer layer where we live. It is made of rock. Even though it feels enormous to us, the crust is really very thin compared to the whole Earth — a bit like the thin skin on the mango. Under the oceans the crust is only about 5 km thick. Under the land it is thicker, about 70 km. At the surface the crust is a comfortable temperature, around 20 degrees Celsius, but deep down at the bottom of the crust it reaches about 400 degrees Celsius.

2. The Mantle. Below the crust is the mantle, and it is very thick — about 3000 km deep. Try to imagine a journey of 3000 km; that is much further than driving from Mogadishu all the way to Cairo! The rocks in the mantle have been heated so much that they have softened and partly melted. This melted rock is called magma, and it can slowly move and flow, almost like very thick honey. Here the temperature rises to about 1000 degrees Celsius.

3. The Core. Right in the centre is the core, about 3400 km thick. The core is not made of rock — it is made of the metals iron and nickel. The core has two parts. The outer core is so hot that the metal is liquid and runny. The inner core is squeezed so tightly by the weight of all the layers pressing down on it that, even though it is unbelievably hot, it stays solid. For a long time scientists thought the inner core was about 5000 degrees Celsius. Then, in 2014, scientists used new equipment in a laboratory and discovered it is closer to 6000 degrees Celsius — that is as hot as the surface of the Sun!

Did You Know? Notice how scientists changed their answer about the core in 2014. This is a wonderful example of how science works. When scientists find better tools and new evidence, they are happy to update what they know. Being ready to learn something new is a sign of a good scientist — and a good student!

You might still be wondering: if nobody can go down to the core, how do scientists feel so sure about these layers? They are like clever detectives. They cannot see the hidden layers, but they can study the clues that the Earth gives them. One important clue comes from earthquakes. When a big earthquake happens, it sends waves of energy right through the whole planet. These waves travel at different speeds through solid rock, softened rock and liquid metal, and they bend and bounce as they pass from one layer to another. By carefully measuring these waves as they come out on the other side of the Earth, scientists can work out what the hidden layers must be made of — just as you might guess what is inside a wrapped gift by shaking it and listening. Another clue is the rock and magma that volcanoes bring up from below, which lets scientists study a real piece of the mantle without digging.
concepts.example: Here is a way to picture all three layers at once. Imagine the Earth is a hard-boiled egg. The thin, cracked eggshell is the crust. The thick white part is the mantle. And the yellow yolk in the middle is the core. Just like a peach or a mango, this egg is only a model — the real Earth is far more amazing and much, much hotter — but it helps you remember the order of the layers: crust on the outside, mantle in the middle, core at the centre.

concepts.title: Volcanoes
concepts.explanation:
Now that you know there is hot, melted magma inside the mantle, you can understand volcanoes. Sometimes a big crack develops in the Earth's crust. Because the magma below is under great pressure, it pushes its way up through that crack. When the magma finally bursts out onto the surface, we say the volcano erupts. Once the magma has reached the surface and is flowing in the open air, we give it a new name: lava. It is the same red-hot rock, just with a different name depending on whether it is inside the Earth (magma) or outside (lava).

This is the exciting link between Part 1 and Part 2: a volcano is the hot inside of the Earth reaching the surface. When you watch a video of glowing lava, you are actually looking at a piece of the mantle that has escaped from deep inside our planet.

Why does the magma push upwards at all? Think about what happens when you squeeze the bottom of a tube of toothpaste: the paste has nowhere to go but up and out of the opening. In a similar way, the weight of all the rock pressing down on the magma, together with gases trapped inside it, puts the magma under enormous pressure. When a weak crack appears in the crust above, the squeezed magma rushes up through it, just like the toothpaste out of the tube. The trapped gases can make the eruption sudden and explosive, throwing ash and rock high into the sky.

Let us name the main parts of a volcano so you could label a diagram:

Magma chamber — a large pool of magma stored deep underground.

Vent — the central pipe or tube that the magma travels up through to reach the surface.

Crater — the bowl-shaped hole at the very top, where the vent widens and the material bursts out.

Lava — the melted rock flowing down the sides after it erupts.

Ash — tiny bits of burnt lava that shoot into the air like grey powder.

Secondary cone — a small 'baby' volcano on the side, formed when magma pushes out through a crack in the slope.

The most common kind of volcano is a composite volcano. It is built up over many eruptions from layers of ash and layers of lava, one on top of another, like the layers of a canjeero stack. These layers form a tall, cone-shaped mountain with smooth sides. Some volcanoes are different: when very runny lava flows out, cools and hardens over and over, it builds a wide, flat shape called a volcanic plateau rather than a tall cone.

Did You Know? Mount Kilimanjaro in Tanzania, the tallest mountain in all of Africa, is a volcano! It was built up over a very long time by erupting lava and ash. Today it is quiet, and its high top is even covered with ice and snow — a frozen cap sitting on top of a mountain born from fire.

Volcanoes are not spread evenly all over the world. They mostly form where there are many cracks in the Earth's crust. The biggest set of these cracks circles the edge of the Pacific Ocean, and because so many volcanoes erupt there it has earned the name the Pacific Ring of Fire. Countries such as Indonesia, the Philippines and Japan sit along this ring and have many volcanoes.

Here in East Africa we have our own special line of cracks: the Great Rift Valley. This is a giant split in the crust that stretches for thousands of kilometres. The Earth's crust here is slowly being pulled apart, which lets magma rise up. That is why the Rift Valley is dotted with volcanoes and volcanic highlands, including Mount Kilimanjaro, Mount Kenya, and the still-active Ol Doinyo Lengai in Tanzania. Places far from any cracks, like the flat middle of a large continent, almost never have volcanoes.

You might think volcanoes only bring death and destruction. It is true that they can be very dangerous. But millions of people choose to live near volcanoes, because volcanoes also bring good things. Let us look at both sides.

The dangers: People can be injured or killed by hot lava and by hard lumps of flying rock. Lava burns and buries crops, animals and homes. Ash covers everything, and breathing in ash or poisonous volcanic gases can make people very ill.
concepts.example: The benefits: When lava and ash break down over the years, they make the soil extremely rich, so crops grow very well on the slopes of old volcanoes. The coffee and banana farms on the fertile volcanic highlands around Kilimanjaro and Mount Kenya are famous for exactly this reason. Deep underground water heated by the magma rises to the surface as hot springs, which people enjoy and which attract visitors. In some countries, this natural underground heat is even used to warm homes and make electricity. Kenya produces a large share of its electricity from this volcanic heat under the Rift Valley!

concepts.title: Earthquakes
concepts.explanation:
The word 'quake' means to shake. So an earthquake is a sudden shaking of the ground. Rub your two hands together quickly right now. Can you feel them getting warm? That warmth is energy made by the two surfaces rubbing. Something similar, but on a giant scale, causes an earthquake.

Two special words help us describe an earthquake. The focus is the exact spot inside the crust where the earthquake begins — where the rocks first slip. The epicentre is the point on the surface directly above the focus. The shaking is usually strongest at the epicentre, so that is where the worst damage happens. Think of dropping a stone into a still pond: the place where the stone hits the water is like the focus, and the ripples spreading out are like the earthquake waves.

Here is another way to picture how the energy stores up and then lets go. Take a fresh green twig from a tree and slowly bend it. At first it just bends and holds, storing up the pushing energy in your hands. But if you keep bending, all of a sudden it snaps — CRACK! — and you feel the shock jump through your fingers. The rocks in the crust are like that twig. They bend and hold under pressure for years, storing energy, until at last they suddenly slip and snap, and all that stored energy shoots out as shaking waves. This is why an earthquake often comes without warning: the rocks were quietly holding their energy until the moment they gave way.

Did You Know? There are about 500,000 earthquakes around the world every single year! Most are so tiny that nobody feels them. Only about 100 each year are strong enough to cause serious damage.

Earthquakes happen in the same places as volcanoes — wherever the rocks of the crust are broken and moving. So the Pacific Ring of Fire has many earthquakes, and so does our own Great Rift Valley. People living in Nairobi, Addis Ababa and other Rift Valley towns sometimes feel small tremors. A large earthquake can also cause a landslide, which is when loose soil and mud slide down a slope and can bury roads, farms or houses below.

What happens if an earthquake occurs under the sea, on the ocean floor? The energy from the shaking passes into the water and can create a tsunami — a huge, powerful sea wave. Out in the deep ocean the wave is not very tall. But as it races toward the shore and the water becomes shallow near the coast, the wave grows taller and taller. When it finally reaches the beach it can be many metres high and floods the coastal land with terrible force.
concepts.example: This is not only something that happens far away. In 2004, a massive earthquake under the Indian Ocean sent a tsunami all the way across the water. It struck the coast of Somalia, damaging fishing villages and harming people as far away as Hafun and the Puntland coast, even though the earthquake began thousands of kilometres away near Indonesia. This shows how the Earth's power in one place can reach coasts all around the same ocean.

concepts.title: Different Habitats
concepts.explanation: The Earth is not only rock and fire. Its surface is covered with living things, and every plant and animal lives in the place that suits it best. A habitat is the natural home of a living thing — the place where it finds the food, the water, the shelter and the space it needs to survive. Living things have special features, called adaptations, that make them suited to their own habitat.
concepts.example: Say this idea back in your own words: The Earth is not only rock and fire. Then find one example of different habitats around your home or outside.

concepts.title: Fish are suited to water
concepts.explanation: Think about a fish, such as the tilapia that swims in the Jubba River or in Rift Valley lakes. A fish cannot live out of water, but it is beautifully suited to living in it. Fish have an organ called gills that lets them breathe by taking oxygen out of the water, and they have fins that help them push through the water and swim fast to escape danger. A fish is perfectly matched to its water habitat.
concepts.example: Say this idea back in your own words: Think about a fish, such as the tilapia that swims in the Jubba River or in Rift Valley lakes. Then find one example of fish are suited to water around your home or outside.

methods.title: Model the Layers of the Earth
methods.example: To build a model that shows the three layers of the Earth — crust, mantle and core — using food from your kitchen.
steps: Look at the whole fruit. This smooth outside is like the Earth's surface.
Ask an adult to carefully cut the fruit in half so you can see inside. (Safety note: only an adult should use the knife.)
Find the three parts. The thin skin is the crust. The thick soft fruit is the mantle. The hard stone in the middle is the core.
Point to each part and say its name out loud.
Draw your cut fruit and label the crust, mantle and core.

methods.title: Build an Erupting Volcano
methods.example: To model how a volcano erupts, using a safe reaction between baking soda and vinegar.
steps: Stand the bottle in the middle of the tray. If you like, pack sand, soil or dough around it to make it look like a mountain, leaving the bottle opening clear at the top.
Put 2 spoons of baking soda into the bottle.
Add a squeeze of dish soap and a few drops of red food colouring, if you have them.
Now the eruption! Pour the vinegar into the bottle and step back to watch. (Safety note: pour gently and keep your face away — the foam can splash. Do not put your eyes close to the opening.)
Watch the red foam bubble up and flow down the sides like lava.

methods.title: The Jelly Earthquake Shake Test
methods.example: To see how the shaking waves of an earthquake can make buildings fall, and to find out what kind of building stands up best.
steps: Place the plate of jelly (or the cushion) on a table. This is your patch of ground.
On top of the jelly, carefully build a tall, thin tower with your blocks.
Next to it, build a short, wide tower using the same number of blocks.
Gently shake or tap the plate from the side to send 'earthquake waves' through the jelly.
Slowly shake a little harder. Watch which tower wobbles and falls first.

methods.title: Bird Beak and Habitat Watch
methods.example: To observe real birds near your home and discover how their beaks are suited to the food in their habitat.
steps: Sit or stand very still and quietly in your chosen spot. (Safety note: stay in a place your family knows is safe, and do not wander near deep water or busy roads.)
Watch carefully and try to spot at least three different birds.
For each bird, look at the shape of its beak — is it small and pointed, long and sharp, flat, or curved?
Notice what the bird is eating or looking for: seeds, insects, fish, or nectar.
Draw the shape of each beak in your notebook.

workedExamples.title: Comparing the Layers
workedExamples.prompt: Sometimes in science we compare numbers to understand size. Let us work through an example together, step by step.
workedExamples.solution:
Question: The mantle is about 3000 km deep. The ocean crust is about 5 km thick. About how many times thicker is the mantle than the ocean crust?

Step 1 — Write down what we know. Mantle depth = 3000 km. Ocean crust thickness = 5 km.

Step 2 — Decide what to do. To find out 'how many times thicker', we divide the bigger number by the smaller number.

Step 3 — Do the division. 3000 divided by 5 = 600.

workedExamples.title: Guided example 2
workedExamples.prompt: The thin, solid outer layer of the Earth where we live is called the: (a) mantle (b) crust (c) core (d) magma
workedExamples.solution: 1 (b) crust The crust is the thin, solid outer rocky layer we live on.

workedExamples.title: Guided example 3
workedExamples.prompt: The very hot centre of the Earth is made mostly of: (a) rock (b) water (c) iron and nickel (d) ice
workedExamples.solution: 2 (c) iron and nickel The core is made of these two metals, not rock.

workedExamples.title: Guided example 4
workedExamples.prompt: Melted rock inside the Earth is called: (a) lava (b) ash (c) magma (d) crust
workedExamples.solution: 3 (c) magma Melted rock inside the Earth is magma.

workedExamples.title: Guided example 5
workedExamples.prompt: Once melted rock erupts onto the surface, we call it: (a) magma (b) lava (c) core (d) mantle
workedExamples.solution: 4 (b) lava The same melted rock is called lava once it erupts onto the surface.

workedExamples.title: Guided example 6
workedExamples.prompt: The bowl-shaped hole at the top of a volcano is the: (a) vent (b) crater (c) focus (d) epicentre
workedExamples.solution: 5 (b) crater The crater is the bowl-shaped hole at the top of the volcano.

workedExamples.title: Guided example 7
workedExamples.prompt: An earthquake is best described as: (a) a shaking of the ground (b) a hot spring (c) a type of soil (d) a sea wave
workedExamples.solution: 6 (a) a shaking of the ground 'Quake' means shake; an earthquake is the ground shaking.

workedExamples.title: Guided example 8
workedExamples.prompt: The point on the surface directly above where an earthquake begins is the: (a) focus (b) mantle (c) epicentre (d) crater
workedExamples.solution: 7 (c) epicentre The epicentre is on the surface directly above the focus.

activities.title: Model the Layers of the Earth
activities.materials: One round fruit with a stone in the middle, such as a mango, peach or plum (the stone will be the core). OR a ball of dough or playdough with a marble hidden inside.; A butter knife (ask an adult to do the cutting).; A plate.
steps: Look at the whole fruit. This smooth outside is like the Earth's surface.
Ask an adult to carefully cut the fruit in half so you can see inside. (Safety note: only an adult should use the knife.)
Find the three parts. The thin skin is the crust. The thick soft fruit is the mantle. The hard stone in the middle is the core.
Point to each part and say its name out loud.
Draw your cut fruit and label the crust, mantle and core.
Safety: Small objects must never go in your mouth, nose or ears. Keep them away from babies and toddlers.

activities.materials: A small empty bottle or cup (this is the vent).; A tray, large plate or baking dish to catch the mess.; Sand, soil or dough to build a mountain shape around the bottle (optional but fun).; 2 spoons of baking soda (bicarbonate of soda).; Half a cup of vinegar.; A squeeze of dish soap and a few drops of red food colouring (optional, to make it look like lava).; A spoon.
steps: Stand the bottle in the middle of the tray. If you like, pack sand, soil or dough around it to make it look like a mountain, leaving the bottle opening clear at the top.
Put 2 spoons of baking soda into the bottle.
Add a squeeze of dish soap and a few drops of red food colouring, if you have them.
Now the eruption! Pour the vinegar into the bottle and step back to watch. (Safety note: pour gently and keep your face away — the foam can splash. Do not put your eyes close to the opening.)
Watch the red foam bubble up and flow down the sides like lava.

activities.title: The Jelly Earthquake Shake Test
activities.materials: A plate or tray of set jelly (jello), OR a firm cushion or folded towel. This is the wobbly ground (the Earth's crust).; Some small blocks, sugar cubes, dry biscuits, or building bricks to make little towers.; Your hands to make the shaking.
steps: Place the plate of jelly (or the cushion) on a table. This is your patch of ground.
On top of the jelly, carefully build a tall, thin tower with your blocks.
Next to it, build a short, wide tower using the same number of blocks.
Gently shake or tap the plate from the side to send 'earthquake waves' through the jelly.
Slowly shake a little harder. Watch which tower wobbles and falls first.

activities.title: Bird Beak and Habitat Watch
activities.materials: A garden, a field, a rooftop, a riverbank or any open space where birds visit.; A notebook and pencil to record what you see.; Patience and a quiet voice so you do not scare the birds away.
steps: Sit or stand very still and quietly in your chosen spot. (Safety note: stay in a place your family knows is safe, and do not wander near deep water or busy roads.)
Watch carefully and try to spot at least three different birds.
For each bird, look at the shape of its beak — is it small and pointed, long and sharp, flat, or curved?
Notice what the bird is eating or looking for: seeds, insects, fish, or nectar.
Draw the shape of each beak in your notebook.

activities.title: Observe: Fish are suited to water
activities.materials: One round fruit with a stone in the middle, such as a mango, peach or plum (the stone will be the core). OR a ball of dough or playdough with a marble hidden inside.; A butter knife (ask an adult to do the cutting).; A plate.
steps: Look for an example of fish are suited to water around your home or outside.
Watch it closely for a few minutes and note three things you notice.
Write or draw what you observed, using the words Crust and Mantle.
Explain your finding out loud, as if you were teaching it. Say it to a family member or your teacher if someone is nearby, or explain it to yourself and check it against the concept explanations.

rules.title: Plates of the Earth's Crust
rules.text: Remember that the Earth's crust is not one smooth shell. It is broken into huge pieces of flat rock, like a cracked eggshell. Where two of these giant pieces meet, they push and rub against each other. Usually they are stuck. But pressure builds and builds until suddenly the rocks slip and move. This sudden movement makes a huge amount of energy, and the energy travels outwards as waves. The waves race through the crust to the surface, and when they reach us we feel the ground shake. That is an earthquake.

terms: Crust
The thin, solid rocky outer layer of the Earth where we live.
Mantle
The thick layer below the crust, made of very hot, softened rock.
Magma
Melted rock inside the Earth that can flow slowly.
Lava
Magma that has erupted and now flows on the surface.
Core
The Earth's very hot centre, made of iron and nickel.
Model
A copy or picture that helps us understand something we cannot easily see.
Volcano
A place where magma erupts through the crust onto the surface.
Vent
The central pipe magma travels up inside a volcano.
Crater
The bowl-shaped hole at the top of a volcano.
Ash
Tiny bits of burnt lava thrown into the air during an eruption.
Earthquake
A sudden shaking of the ground caused by rocks slipping in the crust.
Focus
The place inside the crust where an earthquake begins.

commonMistakes: Thinking the crust is very thick.
The crust is really thin compared to the Earth.
Thinking magma and lava are different things.
They are the same melted rock.
Thinking earthquakes open up huge cracks that swallow people.
Thinking a tsunami is made by wind.
A tsunami is not a wind wave.
Thinking any animal can live anywhere.
Each animal is suited to a habitat.

selfAssessment: I can by the end of this unit, you will be able to:
I can describe the three main layers of the Earth — the crust, the mantle and the core — and say what each layer is made of.
I can explain how scientists use models to understand the inside of the Earth, and why a model is never a perfect copy of the real thing.
I can describe how a volcano forms and name its main parts: the vent, the crater, the lava and the ash.
I can explain what causes an earthquake and how the shaking travels as waves to the surface.
I can describe how earthquakes under the sea can cause a tsunami (a giant sea wave).
I can explain how animals and plants are suited to their habitat, using local examples such as the savanna, the coral reef and the mangrove.
I can connect the Earth's hot inside layers to the volcanoes and earthquakes we see at the surface.
